blocks.md:
Retirement might be 50 years away. That's exactly why starting early is so powerful.

**Time does the heavy lifting**
Money you invest early has decades to grow on its own growth. That's compound growth.

**A simple comparison**
Two people each save the same amount every month at the same growth rate.
• One starts at 25.
• One starts at 35.

The early starter usually ends up with much more, even though the difference is only 10 years. Those extra years of growth add up.

**Small is fine**
You don't need a lot to start. Starting is what matters.
**Try this:** Use the tool in Module 2. Compare saving for 40 years with saving for 20.

A 401(k) is a retirement account you get through a job.

**How it works**
You choose a percent of each paycheck to save. It goes straight into your account and gets invested.

**The employer match**
Many employers add money when you save. For example, they might match 50% of what you put in, up to 6% of your pay. That's like a raise just for saving.

**Always try to get the full match.**

**Vesting**
Some employer money only becomes fully yours after you work there a while. Check your plan's rules.

**Limits**
There's a yearly limit on how much you can put in. It changes most years, so check IRS.gov for the current amount.

An **IRA** is an individual retirement account. You open it yourself. You need earned income to put money in.

**Traditional IRA**
You may get a tax break now. You pay tax when you take money out in retirement.

**Roth IRA**
You put in money you've already paid tax on. Qualified withdrawals in retirement are **tax-free**.

**Which is better?**
• Expect a higher tax rate later? Roth often wins.
• Expect a lower tax rate later? Traditional often wins.

Many young people pick Roth, because their tax rate is usually low now.
**Parent tip:** If your teen has a job, a custodial Roth IRA lets them start early. Contributions can't be more than what they earned that year.

blocks.md:
There's no single right number, but some guidelines help.

**Save a steady percent**
Many planners suggest saving about 15% of income for retirement, counting any employer match. If that's too much now, start smaller and raise it each year.

**Think about your future spending**
Many retirees need most of what they spent while working. Some costs drop, like commuting. Others rise, like health care.

**The 4% guideline**
A common rule of thumb says you can withdraw about 4% of your savings in the first year of retirement, then adjust for inflation. It's a starting point, not a promise.

**Check your progress**
Look at your savings once a year. Small changes early make a big difference later.

question.prompt: Your employer matches 50% of what you save, up to 6% of pay. You save 6%. The match adds…
question.explanation: 50% of 6% is 3% of pay, added on top of your own 6%.

blocks.md:
Retirement accounts have rules about when you can take money out.

**Early withdrawals**
Taking money out of a 401(k) or IRA before age 59½ usually means taxes plus a 10% penalty. There are some exceptions.

**Required withdrawals**
For most traditional accounts, you must start taking money out in your 70s. These are called **required minimum distributions**. The age has changed recently, so check IRS.gov.

**Social Security**
You can start benefits as early as 62. Waiting until your full retirement age, or later up to 70, gives a bigger monthly check. For people born in 1960 or later, full retirement age is 67.

**Plan the order**
Many people use a mix of Social Security, savings and accounts in a planned order to make money last.
**Think twice before cashing out a 401(k) when you change jobs.** Rolling it over keeps your money growing.
